extra_misconceptions.fact: Entering an unassessed scene risks creating a second victim; rescuers must survey for hazards before approaching.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rushing immediately to an injured hiker's side is always the fastest way to save a life in the field.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Callers must stay on the line to answer medical triage questions and receive pre-arrival care instructions.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hanging up as soon as you give your street address allows 911 dispatchers to send an ambulance faster.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Wilderness terrain blocks cellular signals, so patrols need satellite beacons and written evacuation plans.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cell phones with one bar of signal are reliable enough to replace satellite messengers in remote canyons.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Bloodborne pathogens can exist without visible symptoms, requiring nitrile gloves for every bleeding exposure.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Disposable medical gloves are unnecessary when rendering first aid to a close friend or family member.

extra_socratic_questions: What sequence of actions must a rescuer follow if an active hazard appears during victim care?
Which clinical sign distinguishes a life-threatening emergency from an urgent injury during triage?
What exact location details and vital coordinates must be logged before calling wilderness dispatch?
Why is it dangerous to touch a bleeding patient before putting on nitrile gloves and eye protection?

extra_misconceptions.fact: High-adventure trips and camps lasting over 72 hours require a physician-signed Part C pre-participation exam.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Part A and Part B of the Annual Health and Medical Record are sufficient for a ten-day backcountry trek.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Emergency kits must stay in an easily reachable top pocket so any patrol member can grab them in seconds.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sealing a patrol first aid kit inside the bottom of a pack keeps sterile dressings clean until needed.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Moisture compromises barrier packaging and breeds bacteria, so wet or torn sterile dressings must be replaced.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Adhesive bandages and gauze pads remain sterile indefinitely even after their paper wrappers get damp.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Non-prescription medications require documented parental consent on Part B and verification of drug allergies.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Over-the-counter pain relievers in a patrol kit can be given freely to any Scout with a headache.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a patrol leader store Annual Health and Medical Records so they stay dry yet accessible?
What distinguishes the medical authorization in Part A from the physical exam requirement in Part C?
Which expiration dates and dosage metrics must be verified when inspecting a Scout's personal kit?
Under what condition does an expired tetanus immunization change wound follow-up after a trail cut?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Intact blisters form a sterile biological barrier over damaged dermis, and puncturing them invites severe infection.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Popping a fluid-filled burn blister relieves pressure and speeds up skin regeneration on the trail.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Acid-base neutralization generates exothermic heat that deepens tissue burns; flush chemical splashes only with water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Neutralizing an acid burn on the skin with baking soda or vinegar stops chemical damage safely.

extra_misconceptions.fact: High-voltage current travels along nerves and blood vessels, causing deep muscle necrosis and cardiac arrhythmias.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Electrical burns with a tiny entry mark on the fingers involve only minor surface tissue damage.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Direct ice causes frostbite, so cold packs must be wrapped in cloth and applied for 20-minute intervals.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Placing an ice pack directly against bare skin for an hour is the best way to shrink a hematoma.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to brush dry chemical powder off skin with a bare hand instead of flushing with water?
Which physical indicator separates a partial-thickness thermal burn from a full-thickness char injury?
What skin color and capillary refill changes confirm that a severe contusion is causing internal bleeding?
Under what condition does an electrical burn victim become safe for a rescuer to touch and examine?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Leaning back drains blood into the throat and stomach, causing choking or vomiting; pinch the nose and lean forward.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tilting the head backward during a nosebleed prevents blood loss and helps the nasal vessels clot.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Peeling off the bottom dressing rips away newly formed clots; stack fresh gauze pads on top and press firmly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Removing blood-soaked gauze pads to apply fresh dressings helps keep a heavily bleeding wound clean.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Releasing a tourniquet in the field causes fatal exsanguination and dislodges clots; only a physician should remove it.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Loosening a tourniquet every fifteen minutes saves the lower limb from permanent tissue ischemia.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Harsh antiseptics destroy healthy white blood cells and delay healing; irrigate open wounds with clean running water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pouring full-strength hydrogen peroxide or rubbing alcohol into a deep cut sterilizes the tissue safely.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position a windlass tourniquet relative to a spurting arterial wound on the calf?
What visual bleeding pattern distinguishes a severed artery from steady venous hemorrhage in a deep cut?
Why must the exact minute of tourniquet application be written on the strap and the victim's forehead?
What happens to underlying blood vessels if a rescuer pulls out an impaled branch instead of stabilizing it?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Forceful coughing is the most effective way to expel a partial blockage; intervene only if the victim cannot speak or cough.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Slapping a coughing person on the back helps clear a mild airway obstruction faster than coughing alone.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Antihistamines work too slowly to reverse airway swelling or shock; intramuscular epinephrine must be given immediately.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Oral antihistamines like diphenhydramine can replace an epinephrine auto-injector during anaphylaxis.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Ascending with acute mountain sickness triggers fatal brain or lung edema; the victim must stop and descend if worse.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pushing through a throbbing headache and nausea by hiking higher helps a Scout acclimate to altitude.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Carbon monoxide is completely odorless and colorless, binding to hemoglobin and causing hypoxia without warning.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Carbon monoxide gas from a faulty camp stove has a burnt odor that warns sleepers before poisoning occurs.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a rescuer place their fist when delivering abdominal thrusts to a conscious choking adult?
Which respiratory symptom separates mild acute mountain sickness from high-altitude pulmonary edema?
What time interval must be tracked after injecting an epinephrine auto-injector before giving a second dose?
Why is it dangerous to light a camp stove inside a tent vestibule even when the outer flap is cracked open?

extra_misconceptions.fact: It is anatomically impossible to swallow the tongue, and forcing objects into the mouth breaks teeth and blocks airways.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Placing a wallet or wooden spoon between a seizing person's teeth prevents them from swallowing their tongue.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Unconscious patients lack a gag reflex and will aspirate liquids into their lungs; call 911 and maintain the airway.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pouring orange juice or sugary soda into an unconscious diabetic's mouth restores blood sugar safely.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Human bodies do not store electricity after a lightning strike, so rescuers can begin CPR immediately if the scene is safe.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Victims struck by lightning carry a residual electrical charge that shocks anyone who touches them.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Hyperventilation purges carbon dioxide without adding oxygen, suppressing the urge to breathe until blackout occurs.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Taking several deep, rapid breaths before diving underwater increases the oxygen stored in the bloodstream.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a rescuer position an unresponsive breathing victim who has no suspected spinal trauma?
Which clinical behavior distinguishes a conscious hypoglycemic Scout from one who cannot safely swallow glucose?
What seizure duration threshold confirms status epilepticus and requires immediate emergency evacuation?
Under what condition does hyperventilating before a breath-hold swim trigger an underwater hypoxic blackout?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Many victims, especially women and diabetics, experience jaw ache, back pain, shortness of breath, or unexplained nausea.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Heart attacks always present with sudden, crushing pain radiating down the left arm in every victim.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Chewing non-coated aspirin allows rapid absorption into the bloodstream to inhibit platelet clumping when approved.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swallowing a whole coated aspirin tablet with water is the fastest way to limit clot growth during chest pain.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An AED analyzes the heart rhythm automatically and will only charge or deliver a shock for specific fatal arrhythmias.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Automated external defibrillators can accidentally shock a patient whose heart is still beating normally.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Agonal gasps are brainstem reflexes during cardiac arrest that do not oxygenate blood; start CPR immediately.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Occasional snorting or reflex gasps mean a collapsed victim is breathing enough to delay chest compressions.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should AED pads be placed on an adult chest, and what must happen before pressing the shock button?
What physiological mechanism separates a myocardial infarction from sudden cardiac arrest in a patient?
What compression rate and chest depth measurements confirm high-quality adult CPR on a training manikin?
Why is it dangerous to mistake agonal gasps for normal breathing when deciding whether to start chest compressions?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tendons and nerves often remain intact across non-displaced fractures, so painless motion does not rule out a break.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Moving fingers or toes means an injured limb is only sprained and cannot have a broken bone.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Forcing a dislocated joint in the field can pinch arteries or fracture bone; splint the limb in the position found.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Popping a dislocated shoulder or finger joint back into its socket on the trail prevents nerve damage.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Overtightened ties cut off circulation as swelling increases; splints must be snug yet allow distal pulse and sensation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tying splint cravats as tightly as possible keeps a fractured tibia from shifting during a litter carry.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Heat dilates blood vessels and worsens internal bleeding during the first 48 hours; apply wrapped cold packs instead.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Applying a hot pack immediately to a freshly sprained ankle relaxes the ligaments and reduces swelling.

extra_socratic_questions: Where must a rigid splint extend relative to the joints above and below a suspected forearm fracture?
Which anatomical tissue is damaged in a ligament sprain compared to a muscle strain or tendon rupture?
What distal pulse, motor, and sensory checks must be recorded before and after tying a splint in place?
Why is it dangerous to push a protruding bone end back inside an open fracture wound before splinting?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Physical exertion and jostling worsen brain swelling and neck trauma; keep the patient still and monitor responsiveness regularly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Keeping a concussed victim awake by shaking them or making them walk prevents them from slipping into a coma.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Plugging cerebrospinal fluid drainage raises intracranial pressure; cover the ear or nose loosely with sterile gauze to absorb flow.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Clear fluid draining from the ear or nose after a head blow should be plugged tightly with sterile gauze pads.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Patients with unstable spinal fractures can still move their limbs initially before shifting bone fragments sever the spinal cord.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Normal movement in the fingers and toes proves that a fall victim has not fractured any vertebrae in the neck.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Leave a fitted helmet in place to stabilize the cervical spine unless it blocks airway access or prevents rescue breathing.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Removing a snug climbing or bicycling helmet right away is required to inspect the scalp and check the airway.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to apply firm direct pressure directly over a soft or depressed area of a bleeding scalp wound?
Which physical indicator distinguishes a leaking skull fracture from an ordinary nosebleed after a fall onto rocky terrain?
What specific changes in pupil size, speech clarity, and orientation must you log every fifteen minutes after a head impact?
Where should a rescuer position both hands and knees to maintain manual inline stabilization before a cravat bandage is tied?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pulling a patient sideways bends and twists the vertebral column; always drag the body lengthwise along the line of the shoulders.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Dragging an unresponsive patient sideways by the belt or waist is the fastest way to clear an immediate hazard.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Upper-body carries compress the shoulder girdle and ribs; never use a pack-strap carry on someone with arm, rib, or spine injuries.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Carrying a conscious hiker in a pack-strap carry works well even when the hiker has a suspected collarbone fracture.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Unless fire, rising water, or falling rock threatens life immediately, splint all fractures where the victim lies before moving them.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Moving a fracture victim to a shaded tent before splinting saves time and keeps the rescue area better organized.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Bending at the waist strains the lower back and risks dropping the litter; squat with a straight back and lift using leg muscles.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Lifting a stretcher by bending at the waist gives bearers better visibility of rocks and roots along a narrow trail.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a rescuer position a victim's forearms during a shoulder drag to minimize twisting along the long axis of the spine?
Under what condition does a two-handed seat carry become necessary instead of a four-handed seat during a two-rescuer carry?
What distal circulation and sensation checks must you record before and after securing an injured hiker onto an improvised litter?
What load test confirms that an improvised pole-and-jacket stretcher will not tear before lifting an injured patient off the ground?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Excessive plain water without salt dilutes blood sodium levels and causes dangerous brain swelling known as hyponatremia.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Drinking several liters of plain water rapidly on a hot hike prevents both heat cramps and electrolyte depletion.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Exertional heat stroke patients often continue sweating; altered mental status, confusion, or collapse is the defining warning sign.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A hiker who is still sweating heavily on a humid afternoon cannot be suffering from life-threatening heat stroke.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Fever medications do not reset heat-overloaded thermoregulation and can damage the liver and kidneys; use rapid external cooling.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Giving aspirin or acetaminophen lowers the dangerous core temperature of a camper experiencing classic heat stroke.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Refreezing thawed tissue causes catastrophic ice-crystal cell destruction; never thaw frostbitten feet if refreezing is possible.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Thawing frostbitten toes inside a warm tent even when the hiker must walk out in freezing snow saves the tissue.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to core organ survival when rescuers delay cold-water immersion or ice-pack application on a heat stroke victim?
Which physical indicator separates exercise-associated over-hydration from severe dehydration in a confused, nauseated trail hiker?
What intake volume and mental status observations should a patrol leader log when rehydrating a camper with heat exhaustion?
Why is it dangerous to rub frostbitten fingers with snow or warm them directly beside a campfire instead of using warm water?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Paper-bag rebreathing dangerously reduces oxygen intake and masks asthma or cardiac problems; use coached slow breathing instead.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Breathing into a paper bag is the safest field remedy whenever an anxious camper begins breathing rapidly at camp.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Coercing a panicked person triggers sympathetic overload and unsafe movements on belay; pause, validate feelings, and restore choice.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Forcing a terrified Scout onto a high ropes element right away cures their fear of heights through rapid exposure.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Direct, compassionate questions about self-harm reduce isolation and allow you to connect the person with immediate adult help.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Asking a distressed friend directly whether they are thinking about self-harm plants the idea in their mind.

extra_misconceptions.fact: High sympathetic arousal diverts blood to large muscles and causes hand tremors that degrade fine motor dexterity under stress.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Adrenaline surges during an emergency always sharpen fine motor coordination for tying knots or opening bandages.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to heart rate and carbon dioxide balance when a panicked climber slows each exhalation during paced breathing?
Which behavioral indicator shows that a Scout's pre-rappel nervousness has escalated into an acute freeze response on the ledge?
What breathing rate and hand sensation changes confirm that a hyperventilating camper is recovering from an acute stress reaction?
Where should a buddy position a panicked Scout relative to cliff edges or belay hardware before starting grounding exercises?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tap water and scrubbing destroy fragile periodontal ligament cells on the root; handle only the crown and store the tooth in milk.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Scrubbing dirt off the root of a knocked-out tooth with soap and tap water prepares it for clean reimplantation.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Both eyes move together in conjugate gaze; cover both eyes when an object is impaled so darting eye movements do not worsen injury.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Bandaging only the injured eye leaves the uninjured eye free so the patient can walk along the trail unaided.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Solid food and high-sugar drinks irritate inflamed stomach lining and worsen diarrhea; start with small, frequent sips of oral fluids.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Giving solid food and sports drinks immediately after a bout of food-poisoning vomiting restores lost stomach energy.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Heat increases inflammation and can hasten appendix rupture; never apply heat or give food, laxatives, or pain pills for acute pain.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Placing a warm heating pad over a rigid, tender lower-right abdomen relieves cramping from suspected appendicitis.

extra_socratic_questions: Which direction should sterile saline flow across the bridge of the nose when flushing a grit particle from a camper's right eye?
Which physical indicator during a FAST check distinguishes an acute stroke from simple facial numbness caused by cold wind?
Why is it critical to record the exact clock time when a stroke victim was last seen speaking and moving normally?
Why is it dangerous to scrub the root of a knocked-out permanent tooth or store it in tap water during transport to a dentist?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The Demonstrate step requires performing the physical skill live step by step at a visible pace so learners see proper hand placement.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Showing a first-aid video or reading the merit badge pamphlet aloud fulfills the Demonstrate step of the EDGE method.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Doing the task for the learner prevents muscle memory; during the Guide step, coach verbally while the learner keeps hands on the gear.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Taking the bandage out of a struggling Scout's hands to finish the knot for them speeds up the Guide stage effectively.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Live abdominal thrusts and chest compressions can fracture ribs or damage organs in healthy volunteers; use manikins or simulated cues.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Practicing real abdominal thrusts or full-pressure chest compressions on a healthy buddy builds realistic rescue strength.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The Enable stage requires learners to perform the first-aid skill independently under realistic conditions without relying on prompts.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Passing the Enable step means a Scout repeated the steps once while reading from a printed checklist on the table.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to learner skill retention when an instructor jumps straight from verbal explanation to independent testing?
Which coaching behavior separates the Guide stage from the Enable stage when teaching Scouts to tie an arm sling?
What observable performance criteria confirm that a Scout has mastered applying a pressure bandage during the Enable stage?
Why is it dangerous to tighten an actual windlass tourniquet fully on a healthy partner's arm during a practice demonstration?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Emergency Medical Technicians provide basic life support, while Paramedics complete advanced clinical training for invasive procedures.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every ambulance responder carries the same certification level and can administer intravenous drugs or intubate patients.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Dispatchers send units while you are still talking and stay on the line to give pre-arrival life-saving instructions until crews arrive.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hanging up as soon as you give the street address lets the 911 dispatcher send the ambulance crew to the scene faster.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Crews first perform a scene size-up and don personal protective equipment to ensure hazards do not injure the rescue team.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: First responders rush directly to the patient's side the instant the ambulance pulls up to an emergency scene.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Remote terrain, weather, and litter carry logistics often delay EMS extraction for hours, making sustained Scout first aid vital.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wilderness search and rescue ambulances can reach a backcountry patient within ten minutes of a cell phone 911 call.

extra_socratic_questions: What critical patient history and timeline details should a Scout deliver first when handing care over to arriving paramedics?
Which life-saving interventions distinguish an Advanced Life Support paramedic unit from a Basic Life Support ambulance crew?
What location coordinates, mechanism of injury, and vital sign trends must you log before calling emergency dispatchers?
Where should Scouts stage gear and bystanders at a trailhead so an incoming ambulance has unobstructed turnaround clearance?
